The word smelt has two separate verb meanings, and they have nothing to do with each other. You need to know both.
Meaning 1: To Extract Metal from Rock (The Main Meaning)

This is the more important and more commonly tested meaning.

To smelt means to heat ore at extremely high temperatures so that the metal inside it melts out and separates from the surrounding rock and waste material.

What is "ore"? Ore is a type of rock that has metal locked inside it. For example, iron ore is a reddish, rocky mineral that contains iron buried within it. The metal doesn't just sit there loose — it is chemically bonded to other substances. Simply breaking or crushing the rock won't free the metal.

What smelting does: When you smelt ore, you put it in a giant furnace and heat it to an intensely high temperature — far beyond what a household fire can produce. At those temperatures, the metal melts, separates from the rocky waste material, and flows out in liquid form. The liquid metal is then collected, cooled, and shaped. The leftover rocky waste that gets discarded is called slag.

Think of it this way: imagine ore as a sponge soaked in juice. You can't just squeeze the sponge gently — you need an extreme process to get the juice out cleanly. Smelting is that extreme process, using heat instead of pressure.

Common examples of smelting:

  • Iron ore is smelted to produce iron and steel.
  • Copper ore is smelted to produce copper.
  • Tin ore is smelted to produce tin.
  • Lead ore is smelted to produce lead.

This is one of the oldest and most important industrial processes in human history. Civilizations that learned to smelt metals could make tools, weapons, and structures that were far stronger than anything made from stone or wood.

Sentences using smelt (Meaning 1):

  • "Workers smelt copper ore in a large furnace."
  • "The ancient Egyptians knew how to smelt gold and copper."
  • "The factory smelted thousands of tons of iron every year."
  • "The ore must be smelted at temperatures exceeding 1,500 degrees."

Key related words:

  • A smelter — either the person who smelts metal, or the building/facility where smelting happens (a smelting plant).
  • Smelting — the process itself. ("Smelting is an energy-intensive process.")
  • Smelted — past tense. ("They smelted the ore overnight.")

This is simpler but causes a lot of confusion for learners.

In British English (and also Australian and South African English), smelt is the standard past tense and past participle of the verb to smell.

PresentPast (British)Past (American)

In British English:

  • "I smelled something burning." → more natural to say: "I smelt something burning."
  • "She smelled the flowers." → "She smelt the flowers."

In American English, smelled is the standard form, and "smelt" as a past tense of smell sounds unusual or even incorrect to American ears.

So:

  • "The bread smelt wonderful when it came out of the oven." — perfectly correct British English.
  • "He smelt something strange in the basement." — correct in British English.

Important note: In American English, if you use "smelt" as a past tense of smell, people will understand you, but they may consider it old-fashioned or non-standard. In most formal American writing, "smelled" is safer.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Context will almost always make it obvious:

  • If the sentence involves metal, ore, furnaces, or industrial processes → it's Meaning 1 (extracting metal).
  • If the sentence involves a nose, a scent, an odor, or a fragrance → it's Meaning 2 (past tense of smell).

Compare:

  • "They smelt iron at the factory." → extracting iron from ore.
  • "They smelt iron in the air near the factory." → they detected the smell of iron.

Smelt = Meaning 1: To heat ore at very high temperatures to melt out and extract the pure metal from it. Used globally in both British and American English in this sense.

Smelt = Meaning 2: Past tense of "smell." Used in British English where American English would say "smelled."

The metallurgy meaning (Meaning 1) is the one that appears most often in exams, literature, and general knowledge. The "past tense of smell" meaning (Meaning 2) is the one that trips up learners reading British texts.
